questions.q: What is a Private Endpoint, specifically?
options: A network interface with a private IP address from your own VNet's address space, representing your Azure SQL server as if it lived inside your VNet
A firewall rule that allow-lists a specific IP range
A subnet-level setting that tags outbound traffic with the VNet's identity
A stored procedure used to configure server-level firewall rules
questions.explain: Traffic to a Private Endpoint's private IP never touches the public internet, unlike Lessons 26-27's controls which still gate a public endpoint.

questions.q: What state does a new Private Endpoint connection sit in before the Azure SQL server owner approves it?
options: Pending — the connection exists but traffic isn't flowing yet
Approved by default, with no owner action required
Rejected automatically until manually recreated
Active, but rate-limited to encrypted traffic only
questions.explain: The approval workflow is itself a security control — the VNet side can't silently wire up private connectivity without the server owner's approval.

questions.q: What underlying Azure service makes PaaS resources like Azure SQL reachable via a private IP inside a consumer's VNet?
options: Azure Private Link
Azure Firewall
Azure Front Door
Azure Traffic Manager
questions.explain: Private Link is the mechanism; the Private Endpoint is the specific network object it creates representing your server.

questions.q: What commonly breaks a Private Endpoint setup even after the connection is approved?
options: DNS not resolving the server's name to the new private IP — without a linked privatelink.database.windows.net zone, clients keep resolving to the public IP
TDE not being enabled on the database
The database missing a clustered index
Row-Level Security policies not being defined
questions.explain: A private IP only helps if clients actually resolve to it — this DNS step is one of the most common real-world failure points, covered further in Lesson 30.

questions.q: What does a Private Endpoint remove that a well-configured firewall rule and VNet service endpoint still leave in place?
options: The public endpoint's exposure to the internet entirely — traffic to the private IP never uses a public path, versus rules that still gate an existing public endpoint
The need for any authentication at all after connecting
The requirement to configure Transparent Data Encryption
The need for a VNet to exist in the first place
questions.explain: Firewall rules and service endpoints narrow who can reach the public endpoint; a Private Endpoint removes the public path for that traffic entirely.
